A ball thrown through air feels a drag that grows with the square of its
speed and always points against its velocity. That couples the horizontal and
the vertical motion: how fast the ball slows down horizontally depends on how
fast it is falling, and the other way round. The equations of motion cannot be
solved in closed form. Everything the previous lessons compared their
simulations with is gone.

The question we want answered is still a plain one: at what angle should the
ball be thrown to go furthest? Without drag the answer is $45^\circ$, from a
formula. With drag there is no textbook answer, and the best angle depends
on the ball. A simulation can give one, but it is only worth as much as our
reason to trust the simulation. So before we use it, we check it in the
limiting cases that do have exact answers, without drag and in a long fall,
and by refinement: a result that keeps changing as the time step shrinks is
not a result yet, and the rate at which it stops changing says how far it is
from the limit.

## Assumptions

The model and the program rest on these assumptions. Each one names what
goes wrong when it does not hold.

1. **A point particle without spin.** A spinning ball carries a layer of
   air around with it and feels a sideways force, the Magnus force, that
   makes topspin dip and backspin float. None of that is in the model; a real
   throw with spin lands somewhere else.
2. **Quadratic drag with a constant drag coefficient.** The drag is
   $-\tfrac{1}{2}\rho C_d A\,|\mathbf{v}|\,\mathbf{v}$ with a fixed $C_d$.
   This holds in the Newtonian drag regime, where the drag coefficient of a
   sphere is approximately constant, so that the force scales with the speed
   squared, and the ball leaves a turbulent wake; [the range is of the order of a thousand to a few hundred
   thousand]{.not-verified}, and the first example computes where the tennis
   ball lies in it. At much lower speeds the law becomes linear, as in the
   previous lesson. At higher speeds a smooth sphere reaches the drag crisis,
   where $C_d$ [drops abruptly, by more than half]{.not-verified}; a rough or
   seamed ball reaches it earlier. For a ball thrown that fast the constant
   $C_d$ overestimates the drag. The lesson does not model either end of the
   range.
3. **Still, uniform air.** No wind, and a constant air density. In a wind
   the drag acts on the velocity relative to the air. Density changes with
   altitude by a few per cent per hundred metres, which matters for a shell,
   not for a ball.
4. **Uniform gravity and flat ground at the launch height.** The ranges
   are tens of metres, so the Earth's curvature and rotation are negligible,
   and the ball lands at the height it was thrown from. A throw from a height
   is a one-argument change, shown in the code, but the formula for the
   drag-free range used as a check assumes a launch from the ground.
5. **A first-order method with a small step.** Explicit Euler's error is
   proportional to the time step; the convergence study below measures it.
   The landing point is interpolated linearly within the last step, which
   adds an error proportional to the square of the step, below the method's
   own. As in the previous lesson, a step that is too large makes the method
   unstable. Near a speed $v$ a small change $\delta v$ of the speed obeys
   $\mathrm{d}\,\delta v/\mathrm{d}t \approx -(2c\,v/m)\,\delta v$, which
   is linear drag with the time constant $\tau = m/(2c\,v)$, so the result of
   the previous lesson says the step must stay below $2\tau = m/(c\,v)$. The
   first example puts a number on it, far above every step used.
6. **Round-off is negligible.** The steps are far above the resolution of
   double-precision numbers, so the errors in the tables are the errors of the
   method.

## Drag that grows with the square of the speed {#explanation}

At everyday sizes and speeds a body moving through air leaves a turbulent
wake, and the drag on it is

$$
\mathbf{F}_d = -c\,|\mathbf{v}|\,\mathbf{v},
\qquad
c = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\rho\,C_d\,A,
$$

where $\rho$ is the density of the air, $A$ the cross-section the body
presents to the flow, and $C_d$ a dimensionless **drag coefficient** that
depends on the shape. The constant $c$ has the unit kg/m. The force has the
magnitude $c\,|\mathbf{v}|^2$ and points against the velocity.

A body falling under this drag reaches the **terminal speed** at which the
drag balances the weight, $c\,v_T^2 = m g$, so

$$
v_T = \sqrt{\frac{m g}{c}}.
$$

::: {.go-deeper ref="drag-coefficient-regimes"}
Why the drag is quadratic in the Newtonian drag regime, where the drag
coefficient of a sphere is approximately constant, and linear at
$\mathrm{Re} \ll 1$. The lesson takes the quadratic law as its model and
does not need the page.
:::

The terminal speed is the natural scale of the problem. The ratio of the drag
to the weight at any moment is $|\mathbf{v}|^2 / v_T^2$. A ball thrown much
more slowly than its terminal speed hardly notices the air; a ball thrown at
its terminal speed starts with a drag equal to its weight, and its path looks
nothing like a parabola.

The two laws differ in how fast the drag grows with the speed.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.draw_drag_against_speed)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-drag-against-speed
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Drag against speed for the linear and the quadratic law. The quadratic drag is smaller at low speed and larger above the crossing."
#| fig-status: conceptual
#| fig-alt: "Sketch of drag force against speed. A solid line, the linear law, rises in a straight line from the origin. A dashed curve, the quadratic law, starts flatter and below the line, crosses it, and then climbs above it ever more steeply."
result.show("fig-drag-against-speed")
```

The sketch has no scale, and where the curves cross depends on $b$ and $c$.
It carries the shape: doubling the speed doubles a linear drag and
quadruples a quadratic one.

### Why there is no closed form

With $x$ horizontal and $y$ upward, Newton's second law reads

$$
\begin{aligned}
m\,\frac{\mathrm{d}v_x}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -c\,\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}\;v_x, \\
m\,\frac{\mathrm{d}v_y}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -m g - c\,\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}\;v_y.
\end{aligned}
$$

The square root contains both components, so neither equation can be solved
on its own. For linear drag the factor in front of $v_x$ was the constant
$b$, the components separated, and each was a first-order linear equation
with an exponential solution. Here the factor is the speed itself, which is
unknown until the problem is solved. The motion can be reduced to integrals
by a change of variables, but those integrals have to be evaluated
numerically anyway, and there is no formula to compare a simulation with.
This is an argument that the methods of the previous lessons do not apply,
not a proof that no formula exists, and the lesson does not prove the
latter.

### How to trust a simulation without one

Three checks replace the comparison with an exact solution. Together they are
the validation strategy of this lesson, and of every later one whose problem
has no closed form.

1. **Limiting cases.** Set $c = 0$ and the motion must become the parabola
   of the first lesson, with the range $R_0 = v_0^2 \sin(2\theta) / g$ for a
   launch from the ground at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$. The first lesson
   even predicts how far explicit Euler misses it: the computed height lags
   the exact one by $\tfrac{1}{2} g\,t\,\Delta t$. At the landing time
   $T = 2 v_0 \sin\theta / g$ that lag is $v_0 \sin\theta\,\Delta t$, and
   the ball is falling there with the vertical speed $v_0 \sin\theta$, so it
   needs a time $\Delta t$ more to reach the ground: it lands $\Delta t$ late
   and so about $v_x \Delta t$ too far. A simulation
   that reproduces the parabola with exactly that error is doing what it
   should. The other limit, a long fall, must approach the terminal speed;
   the first exercise checks it. The drag-free limit tests the parts that
   do not involve drag: the launch, the stepping, gravity, and the search for
   the ground. The long fall tests the drag force itself, against the
   terminal speed it must produce.
2. **Convergence.** Compute the range with the step $\Delta t$, then with
   $\Delta t/2$, $\Delta t/4$, and so on. For a first-order method the
   differences between successive results must halve each time, and the
   observed order, $\log_2$ of the ratio of successive differences, must
   tend to one. When it does, the result behaves like
   $R(\Delta t) = R^* + C\,\Delta t$, and two steps determine both unknowns.
   Subtracting $R(\Delta t/2) = R^* + C\,\Delta t/2$ from $R(\Delta t)$ gives
   $C\,\Delta t/2 = R(\Delta t) - R(\Delta t/2)$, and inserting it back gives
   $$
   R^* \approx 2\,R(\Delta t/2) - R(\Delta t),
   \qquad
   R(\Delta t/2) - R^* \approx R(\Delta t) - R(\Delta t/2).
   $$
   This is **Richardson extrapolation**. The first formula estimates the
   limit, the second the error of the finer result, both from the simulation
   alone. This check removes a different doubt from the first: not whether
   the program has the right parts, but how far its number for the throw
   with drag still is from the exact solution of its equations.
3. **Physical sense.** Drag must shorten the range, slow the ball down on the
   way up, and make the descent steeper than the ascent. These checks catch
   sign errors that the first two can miss.

### Finding the ground

The simulation steps in time, and no step ends exactly at the ground. The
loop stops after the first state below it, and the landing point is
interpolated linearly between that state and the one before: if the last
step went from a height $y_1 \ge 0$ to $y_2 < 0$, the crossing happened a
fraction $y_1 / (y_1 - y_2)$ of the way through the step, and the range is
the horizontal position at that fraction. Within one step the path is nearly
straight. Linear interpolation of a function $y(t)$ between two points
$\Delta t$ apart has the error $\tfrac{1}{2}\,\ddot{y}(\xi)\,(t - t_1)(t - t_2)$ for some $\xi$
in the step, and $|(t - t_1)(t - t_2)|$ is largest at the middle of the step,
where it is $\Delta t^2/4$. So the interpolation is off by at most
$\tfrac{1}{8}\,|\ddot{y}|\,\Delta t^2$ in height, far below the first-order
error of the method itself.

The path with drag is not a parabola. It comes down more steeply than it went
up, because the drag has eaten most of the horizontal velocity by then, and
it lands at a steeper angle and a lower speed than it was thrown with.

Two different questions stand behind these numbers. Does the program solve
the equations of the model correctly? And do those equations describe a real
tennis ball? The next two examples test the first. No check of the program
can answer the second; that takes a measurement, and Limits returns to it.

### The drag-free limit

The first check: with $c = 0$ the simulated range must approach the exact
$R_0 = v_0^2 \sin(2\theta)/g$ as the step shrinks, and the first lesson
predicts the error to be about $v_x\,\Delta t$, the horizontal velocity times
the time step.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.drag_free_convergence)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("drag-free-convergence")
```

The error halves with the step and matches the prediction from the first
lesson to within the small interpolation error: at the smallest step the two
differ by `{python} result["prediction-gap"]` m.
The simulation reproduces the one case that can be solved by hand, including
the way it misses it.

### Convergence with drag

With drag there is no exact range to compare with, so the program is compared
with itself. The second check, on the throw with drag: the range at ever smaller
steps, the difference to the previous one, the observed order, and the
Richardson estimate of the limit from each pair of steps.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.richardson)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("richardson")
```

The differences halve and the observed order is
`{python} result["last-order"]` at the finest step, so the method behaves as a
first-order method should on this problem too, and the Richardson estimates
settle on a limit long before the direct results do. The range with drag is
`{python} result["best-estimate"]` m, and the finest direct result is
still `{python} result["error-estimate-mm"]` mm from the previous one. The
Richardson estimate assumes that the error is proportional to the time step;
the observed orders are the check of that assumption, not a proof. On
logarithmic axes the error of the direct results against the extrapolated
limit is a straight line of slope one:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.draw_convergence_of_the_range)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-convergence-of-the-range
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The error of the range with drag falls in proportion to the time step, parallel to the reference line, so the extrapolated limit is a trustworthy reference."
#| fig-status: simulated
#| fig-alt: "Log-log plot of the error of the computed range in metres against the time step in seconds. The points lie on a straight line parallel to a dotted reference line of slope one: the error falls in proportion to the time step, over a wide span of both."
result.show("fig-convergence-of-the-range")
```

### The range against the launch angle

Now the question of the lesson. Before the cell, decide what you expect:
does drag move the best angle, and if so, which way? If drag only scaled
every range down by the same factor, the best angle would stay at
$45^\circ$. Without drag, $45^\circ$ is the balance between time in the air
and horizontal speed. Drag takes away speed for as long as the ball flies,
and a steeper throw flies longer, which suggests a flatter best angle; but a
flatter throw also climbs less and lands sooner. That is an expectation, not
a result, and for this model the simulation decides.

With the simulation checked and its error known, the cell computes the range
for launch angles from $10^\circ$ to
$80^\circ$, with and without drag, using a step at which the convergence table
puts the error well below a decimetre, and then finds the angle of the longest
throw to a tenth of a degree with a one-dimensional minimiser from SciPy.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment, region="scan")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.best_angle)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.longest_throws)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("longest-throws")
```

Without drag the longest throw is at $45^\circ$, as the formula says, and the
simulation finds it to the resolution asked of the minimiser:
`{python} result["best-without"]` degrees. With drag the best angle is
`{python} result["best-with"]` degrees, lower. [With quadratic drag the
longest throw is flatter than $45^\circ$ for this ball.]{.claim
type="numerically-verified" scope="tennis ball at its launch speed"
evidence="fig-range-against-angle"} The shift goes the way the expectation
above suggested, but the lesson does not derive it: the argument gives at
most a direction, and the size of the shift comes from the simulation, not
from the argument.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.draw_range_against_angle)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-range-against-angle
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "With drag the range is lower, its peak moves to a flatter angle, and the curve is lopsided: a throw that is too steep costs more than one that is too flat."
#| fig-status: simulated
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of range in metres against launch angle in degrees. The drag-free curve is a symmetric arch peaking at a dashed vertical line at the forty-five degree mark. The curve with drag is much lower, peaks a few degrees to the left of the line, and is asymmetric: it falls off more steeply towards high angles than towards low ones."
result.show("fig-range-against-angle")
```

The curve with drag is not only lower but lopsided: it falls off more
steeply towards high angles. How far the best angle moves below $45^\circ$
depends on the ratio of the launch speed to the terminal speed: a ball thrown
much more slowly than its terminal speed hardly notices the air, and the
third exercise puts numbers on that.

So the answer to the question we started with: for this tennis ball, thrown
at about its terminal speed, the longest throw is flatter than $45^\circ$, at
the angle in the table. No formula gave that answer; a simulation did, and
we trust it because the checks showed, for the throw we refined, that the
program solves its equations to an error we can state. They did not show that
the equations describe a real tennis ball: the answer belongs to a model
without spin or wind and with a constant drag coefficient.

## Limits {#limits}

- The model has a constant drag coefficient, no spin, no wind, and flat
  ground at the launch height (assumptions one to four). The best angle and
  the range found here belong to this model of a tennis ball, not to a real
  throw; the lesson compares the simulation with no measurement.
- The Reynolds-number ranges and the drag crisis are order-of-magnitude
  statements marked as not verified in the lesson, and the one source of the
  register supports only the form of the two force laws.
- The convergence study shows that the error behaves like a first-order error
  for one throw. The Richardson estimate assumes this; other throws, such as
  a very steep one, are not checked.
- Validation by limiting cases and refinement shows that the program solves
  its equations, not that the equations describe a ball. Only an experiment
  could show the second.

::: {.exercise .self-check}
The simulated range with drag changes by less than a millimetre when the time
step is halved once more. Does that show that the range of a real tennis ball
thrown like this is known to a millimetre?

::: {.choices}
::: {.choice}
Yes. The method has converged, so the range is correct to that precision.

::: {.feedback}
Not quite: convergence shows that the program solves its equations to that
precision. The equations have a constant drag coefficient and no spin or wind.
:::
:::

::: {.choice correct="true"}
No. It shows that the numerical error of this model is below a millimetre;
the model itself is not that accurate.

::: {.feedback}
Correct: convergence measures the error of the method, and the assumptions of
the model, such as a constant drag coefficient, are a different and larger
source of error.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
No. A first-order method cannot reach that precision.

::: {.feedback}
Not quite: a first-order method reaches any precision at enough steps, at a
cost that grows in proportion; the second exercise measures it.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.solution}
The refinement and the Richardson estimate bound the error between the
simulation and the exact solution of the model's equations. They say nothing
about the difference between the model and the thrown ball: the drag
coefficient is an input of about the right size, and the spin and the wind are
absent. The real range is uncertain by far more than a millimetre.
:::
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
**The other limit.** Drop the tennis ball from rest from a great height and
let it fall for 15 s. Check that its speed approaches the terminal speed
derived above, and find the time at which it reaches 95 per cent of it. Use
a time step of 1 ms.

::: {.solution}
On a vertical line with down positive the acceleration is
$g - (c/m)\,v\,|v|$, and the same functions run it with one-component
vectors.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.terminal_fall)
```

The terminal speed from the formula is `{python} result["terminal-speed-3"]` m/s;
the speed after `{python} result["fall-time"]` s of falling is
`{python} result["final-speed"]` m/s, and [95 per cent]{.given} of the terminal speed is
reached after `{python} result["reached"]` s. The speed creeps up to the
terminal speed and stays below it, as it must: once the drag balances the
weight there is no force left to accelerate the ball. The natural time scale
is $v_T / g$, the time gravity alone would need to produce the terminal
speed; [95 per cent]{.given} of it is reached after
`{python} result["reached-in-time-constants"]` of those.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
**A step for a millimetre.** From the convergence table, which time steps
give a computed range with drag that is within 1 cm of the limit, without
extrapolation? How small must the step be for 1 mm? Read the first answer
from the Richardson error estimates in the table, and find the second by
continuing the halving until the estimate drops below 1 mm.

::: {.solution}
The error estimate of each result is its difference to the previous one, and
the estimates halve with the step, so every extra decimal digit costs a
little more than three halvings.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.refine)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("refinement")
```

The steps of the table with an estimated error below one centimetre are the
`{python} result["within-a-centimetre"]` finest, from
`{python} result["first-within"]` s down. A millimetre needs a step of
`{python} result["millimetre-step-ms"]` ms, that is
`{python} result["millimetre-steps"]` steps for one throw.
That is still cheap here, but a first-order method pays for every extra digit
with ten times the work. The integrators lesson introduces methods that get
the same digit for a small fraction of the steps.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
**A heavier ball.** A steel ball of the same diameter as the tennis ball has
a mass of about 1.23 kg, so the same drag constant and a terminal speed
several times higher. Thrown at the same 25 m/s, by what fraction does drag
shorten its range at 45 degrees, and where is its best angle? Compare with
the tennis ball and explain the difference with the ratio of launch speed to
terminal speed.

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.steel_and_tennis)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("steel-and-tennis")
```

For the steel ball the drag at launch is
`{python} result["steel-drag-per-cent"]` per cent of the
weight, so the path is nearly a parabola, the range is shortened by
`{python} result["steel-lost"]` per cent, and the
best angle is just below $45^\circ$. The tennis ball, thrown at its terminal
speed, loses `{python} result["tennis-lost"]` per
cent of its range, and its best angle moves several degrees down. The one
number that matters is $(v_0 / v_T)^2$, the drag over the weight at launch:
it is set by the launch speed and the mass, size, and shape of the ball, and
it is why a shot put is thrown as if there were no air while a shuttlecock is
not.
:::
:::
